blocks.title: Introduction
blocks.content:
In 1953, Roth proved that every subset of the integers of positive upper density contains a nontrivial three-term arithmetic progression. This can be stated in the following finite form.

::: theorem
[]{#thm:roth label="thm:roth"} For every $\alpha>0$, if $N$ is sufficiently large, then every set $A\subset\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\}$ with $\lvert A\rvert\geq\alpha N$ contains a three-term arithmetic progression $x,\,x+r,\,x+2r$ with $r\neq 0$.
:::

Roth's theorem is a foundational result in density Ramsey theory; its extension to longer arithmetic progressions is a celebrated theorem of Szemerédi  [@Sz

blocks.title: Front matter
blocks.content:
A FOURIER-FREE DENSITY-INCREMENT PROOF OF
ROTH’S THEOREM
MARK LEWKO
Abstract. We give an elementary, Fourier-free proof of Roth’s theorem.
The proof follows Roth’s original density-increment strategy, but replaces
the usual Fourier-analytic step with a direct combinatorial argument
involving averages over sub-progressions.

blocks.title: Notation
blocks.content: We write $A\lesssim B$ to mean $A\leq CB$ for a positive absolute constant $C$, and similarly $A\gtrsim B$. We write $A\sim B$ when both $A\lesssim B$ and $B\lesssim A$ hold. All implicit constants are absolute. For a prime $m$, write $\mathbb{Z}_m=\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_m^\times=\mathbb{Z}_m\setminus\{0\}$.

blocks.title: Preliminaries
blocks.content:
Write $[N]=\{0,\ldots,N-1\}$ and choose a prime $m$ with $4N<m<8N$, which we may do by Bertrand's postulate. We embed $[N]$ in $\mathbb{Z}_m$ in the obvious way. The point of choosing $m>2N$ is that a three-term progression in $\mathbb{Z}_m$ whose terms all lie in $[N]$ is a genuine integer progression.

blocks.title: No progressions imply large energy
blocks.content: For functions $f_1,f_2,f_3\colon\mathbb{Z}_m\to\mathbb R$, define $$\Lambda(f_1,f_2,f_3):=\sum_{x,r\in\mathbb{Z}_m} f_1(x)f_2(x+r)f_3(x+2r).$$ If $A\subset [N]\subset\mathbb{Z}_m$, then $\Lambda(\mathbf{1}_A,\mathbf{1}_A,\mathbf{1}_A)$ is the number of three-term arithmetic progressions in $A$, including the trivial progressions with $r=0$. Hence, if $A$ contains no nontrivial three-term progressions, then $\Lambda(\mathbf{1}_A,\mathbf{1}_A,\mathbf{1}_A)=\lvert A\rvert$. blocks.title: Large energy implies a modular density increment
blocks.content:
Our next goal is to find a long modular progression on which $f$ has positive average. For an integer $1\leq \ell<m/2$ and a step $d\in\mathbb{Z}_m$, set $$S_d(x):=\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}f(x+id),\qquad V_d:=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_m}\lvert S_d(x)\rvert^2.$$ Thus $S_d(x)$ is the sum of $f$ on the length-$\ell$ modular progression starting at $x$ with step $d$, and $V_d$ is the second moment of these sums as $x$ varies.

blocks.title: Finding a genuine integer progression
blocks.content:
We now show how to pass from a density increment on a modular progression to one on a genuine integer progression.

::: lemma
[]{#lem:rect label="lem:rect"} Suppose $d\in\mathbb{Z}_m^\times$ and $x\in\mathbb{Z}_m$ satisfy $\sum_{i=0}^{\ell-1}f(x+id)\geq\eta\ell$ for some $0<\eta\leq1$. If $\ell\gtrsim\eta^{-2}$, then there is an arithmetic progression $P\subset[N]$ such that $$\lvert P\rvert\gtrsim\eta\sqrt{\ell}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{\lvert A\cap P\rvert}{\lvert P\rvert}\geq\alpha+c\eta$$ for an absolute constant $c>0$.
:::

blocks.title: Proof of Roth's theorem and the quantitative bound
blocks.content:
::: proof
*Proof of Theorem [\[thm:roth\]](#thm:roth){reference-type="ref" reference="thm:roth"}.* Fix $\alpha_0>0$ and suppose, for contradiction, that there are arbitrarily large $N$ and 3AP-free sets $A\subset[N]$ with $\lvert A\rvert\geq\alpha_0N$. Applying Proposition [\[prop:increment\]](#prop:increment){reference-type="ref" reference="prop:increment"}, then rescaling the progression it gives back to an interval, produces a new 3AP-free set with density increased by at least $c\alpha_0^{11}$. Repeating this, the density exceeds $1$ after $O(\alpha_0^{-11})$ steps.

blocks.title: Further remarks
blocks.content:
Although the proof above is written without Fourier analysis, several of the steps have a simple Fourier interpretation. Let $e(x)=e^{2\pi i x/m}$ and $\widehat f(\xi)=\sum_{x\in\mathbb{Z}_m} f(x)e(-\xi x)$. One then has $\widehat R(\xi)=\lvert\widehat f(\xi)\rvert^2$.
